unit_title: Unit 3: Environmental Protection - Grammar Focus (Modal Verbs)
content: Unit 3: Grammar Focus - Modal Verbs & Environmental Protection (Communicative English Skills II - EnLa102) ========================================= 1. CORE CONCEPTS AND FUNDAMENTALS OF MODAL VERBS ========================================= What are Modal Verbs in English Grammar? Modal verbs are specialized auxiliary (helping) verbs that express the speaker's attitude, judgment, or mood regarding the action of the main verb. Unlike standard verbs, modal verbs do not describe standalone actions; instead, they modify the main verb to convey concepts such as ability, obligation, permission, possibility, necessity, certainty, and prohibition (የድርጊቱን ሁኔታ፣ አቅም፣ ግዴታ፣ ስሜት ወይም እርግጠኝነት የሚገልጹ ልዩ ረዳት ግሶች ናቸው)። Key Structural Rules & Features of Modal Verbs: 1. Invariant Form (No Conjugation / No Agreement Changes): Modal verbs never change their form regardless of the subject pronoun (I, he, she, it, we, they). They do NOT take third-person singular suffixes (-s / -es), past tense endings (-ed), or continuous forms (-ing). - Correct: She can speak English. / They can speak English. - Incorrect: She cans speak English. / He caning speak... 2. Followed by Bare Infinitive (Base Form - V1): Pure modal verbs are directly followed by the bare infinitive (the base form of the main verb without 'to'). - Correct: We must protect the ecosystem. - Incorrect: We must to protect the ecosystem. - Note on Semi-Modals: Semi-modal structures such as ought to, have to, and be able to include 'to' as an inherent part of their structure. 3. Direct Negation without Auxiliary Verbs: Negatives are formed simply by adding 'not' directly after the modal verb (often contracted in spoken/informal written English: can't, mustn't, couldn't, shouldn't). They do NOT use do/does/did. - Correct: You should not (shouldn't) waste water. - Incorrect: You don't should waste water. 4. Question Formation via Inversion: To ask questions, modal verbs invert positions with the subject pronoun. - Structure: [Modal Verb] + [Subject] + [Base Verb V1]? - Example: Can we reverse climate damage? / Must they pay the environmental fee? 5. Absence of Participle or Infinitive Forms: Modal verbs cannot function as infinitives (to can, to must) or past/present participles (canned, musting). Instead, alternative structures are used when infinitives or perfect tenses are needed (e.g., using to be able to instead of to can; using to have to instead of to must). ========================================= 2. COMPREHENSIVE MODAL VERBS MATRIX, FUNCTIONS & SPECIAL CASES ========================================= A. Expressing Ability & Capacity (ችሎታንና አቅምን መግለጽ) - Present/General Ability: Uses can / am, is, are able to. - Concept: Describes general skills, physical capacity, or acquired knowledge in the present. - Example: Environmental scientists can predict rainfall patterns with advanced satellite data. - Past General Ability: Uses could / was, were able to. - Concept: Refers to a general capability or skill possessed over a period in the past. - Example: In past decades, local farmers could rely on predictable seasonal rains. - Past Specific Achievement / Successful Action: Uses was/were able to or managed to (NOT could). - Crucial Rule: When describing a specific, difficult accomplishment on a single occasion in the past, use was/were able to or managed to. - Example: Despite the severe flood yesterday, the rescue team was able to save (managed to save) all residents. (NOT: could save) B. Expressing Possibility, Probability & Expectation (እድል፣ ግምትና እምነት) - High Present/Future Possibility: Uses may, might, could + V1. - Concept: Indicates that an event is possible now or in the future, but not 100% guaranteed. - Degrees of Certainty: - May: ~50% probability (Moderate possibility). - Might / Could: ~30–40% probability (Slightly lower or remote possibility). - Example: Severe drought may cause agricultural failures in low-elevation zones. (ድርቁ ከፍተኛ የምግብ እጥረት ሊያስከትል ይችላል) - Example: Global temperatures might rise faster if emissions are not restricted. - Rational / Logical Expectation: Uses should / ought to + V1. - Concept: Expresses an expectation based on natural logic, schedules, or normal circumstances. - Example: According to meteorological forecasts, the seasonal rainfall should begin by early next month. C. Expressing Necessity, Obligation & Advice (ግዴታ፣ አስፈላጊነት እና ምክር) - Strong Internal Obligation / Speaker's Authority: Uses must + V1. - Concept: Expresses a personal obligation or conviction felt strongly by the speaker. - Example: We must protect our native wildlife before these species become extinct. - External Obligation / Rules & Laws: Uses have to / has to + V1. - Concept: Expresses an obligation imposed by external authorities, written laws, regulations, or physical reality. - Example: Industrial factories have to pay strict carbon environmental taxes under local legislation. - Strict Prohibition (የተከለከለ ነገር): Uses must not (mustn't) + V1. - Concept: Indicates that an action is strictly forbidden, illegal, or dangerous. - Example: Visitors must not dump chemical waste into public water reservoirs. - Absence of Obligation / Lack of Necessity: Uses don't have to / doesn't have to / needn't + V1. - Concept: Indicates that an action is optional; there is no compulsion to do it. - Example: You don't have to print the report; you can submit the digital file online. - Advice, Duty & Recommendation: Uses should / ought to / had better + V1. - Concept: Recommends a good or sensible course of action. - Special Case (Had better): Had better expresses strong advice with an implicit warning of negative consequences if ignored. - Example: You should wear protective gear in high-pollution industrial zones. - Example: We had better fix the roof leak now, or the upcoming rain will flood the hall. D. Present Logical Deductions & Certainty (ማስረጃ ላይ የተመሰረተ የአሁን መደምደሚያ) - Present Positive Deduction (Strong Certainty ~95-100%): Uses must + V1 or must be + V-ing. - Concept: Used when present physical evidence leads to an unavoidable logical conclusion. - Example: The lights are on and her car is outside; she must be working in her office. (ስልክ የማታነሳው እየሰራች ስለሆነ መሆን አለበት) - Present Negative Deduction / Impossibility (Strong Negative Certainty): Uses can't + V1 or couldn't + V1. - Concept: Used when current evidence proves that something is logically impossible. - Example: There can't be clean drinking water in this well; it is visibly contaminated with industrial runoff. E. Past Deductions, Speculations & Regrets (ያለፈ ነገር ላይ ግምት፣ መደምደሚያ እና ቁጭት) - Past Positive Deduction (Strong Positive Certainty in the Past): Uses must have + Past Participle (V3). - Concept: Concluding that something definitely happened in the past based on strong physical evidence. - Example: The river channel is completely bone-dry; the region must have suffered a massive drought last summer. (ከፍተኛ ድርቅ አጋጥሞት መሆን አለበት) - Past Negative Deduction / Impossibility: Uses can't have / couldn't have + Past Participle (V3). - Concept: Concluding that a past action was logically impossible based on evidence. - Example: The ancient islanders can't have transported those gigantic stone statues without organized group teamwork. (ያለ ህብረት መስራት ሊሆን አይችልም ነበር) - Past Uncertainty / Speculation: Uses may have / might have / could have + Past Participle (V3). - Concept: Guessing or speculating about past possibilities where certainty is lacking. - Example: The original inhabitants may have landed on Easter Island by navigational accident. (በድንገት ደሴቱ ላይ አርፈው ሊሆን ይችላል) - Past Regret / Unfulfilled Obligation: Uses should have / ought to have + Past Participle (V3). - Concept: Expressing regret, criticism, or a sensible past action that was unfortunately omitted. - Example: The local authorities should have reinforced the coastal dams before the hurricane season arrived. (ማጠናከር ነበረባቸው ግን አላደረጉትም) - Past Unnecessary Action: - Didn't need to + V1: Action was not necessary, so it was NOT performed. - Example: It started raining, so I didn't need to water the garden plants. - Needn't have + V3: Action was performed, but it was later realized to be completely unnecessary. - Example: I needn't have brought an umbrella; the weather stayed clear all afternoon. ========================================= 3. TEXTBOOK ACTIVITIES & DETAILED ANSWERS ========================================= Activity 3.6: Reading Comprehension Solutions 1. Observation on Murray River: A collapse of entire ecosystems, dead river red gums, severe man-made and natural drought. 2. Gigalitres: A unit of volume measurement equal to 1,000,000,000 (one billion) litres. 3. Two conflicting groups: Farmers (portrayed as land-clearers) and Environmentalists. 4. Farmer debt status: Rural farmer debt doubled from £10bn in 1999 to £20bn in 2005. 5. Burge family evidence: Old photographs demonstrating that the Murray River experienced dry conditions in past decades prior to current climate debates. 6. Wayne Cockayne's situation: He lost crop revenue for 4 consecutive years, suffered severe depression, and had to pay for water to be trucked in. 7. 'Garden of Eden' vs 'Graveyard': It was previously fertile, lush, and green ('Garden of Eden'), but drought turned the black box eucalyptus trees into dead, dry structures ('graveyard'). 8. Meaning of 'Become nearly a religion': Belief in global warming has turned into an unquestioned dogma or belief system rather than open scientific discourse. 9. Australia's systemic advantage: It possesses a strong economy and single sovereign jurisdiction where competing groups can negotiate peacefully. 10. 'Wry smile' & synonyms: A grimly humorist or ironic smile. Synonyms: subtle smile, smirk, ironic grin. Activity 3.7: Contextual Vocabulary Solutions 1. Changed completely ➔ transformed (ሙሉ በሙሉ የተቀየረ/የተለወጠ) 2. Fell very dramatically ➔ plummeted (በከፍተኛ ሁኔታ የወረደ/የቀነሰ) 3. Reject ➔ refute (ማስተበል/ስህተት መሆኑን በምክንያት ማሳየት) 4. Uncontrolled ➔ rampant (ቁጥጥር የሌለው/በስፋት የተንሰራፋ) 5. Very serious ➔ acute (በጣም ከባድ/አጣዳፊ) 6. Strangely and worryingly ➔ eerily (በሚያስፈራ ሁኔታ ጸጥ ያለ/ስጋት የሚፈጥር) Activity 3.8: Matching Modals to Grammatical Functions 1. Zeberga should call Almaz soon after their first date. ➔ h. advice 2. Almaz should be happy to get his call. ➔ d. rational probability 3. Zeberga calls but she doesn't pick up, she must be working. ➔ e. certainty 4. No problem, he can call her back later. ➔ i. capacity 5. Later he tells her they could go out to dinner again. ➔ j. suggestion 6. She says she may be available Friday. ➔ b. possibility 7. Zeberga asks if he can call her back Friday morning. ➔ g. permission 8. She says she could be in a meeting, the afternoon is better. ➔ c. low probability 9. Friday afternoon, Zeberga asks: May I pick you up at 6 pm? ➔ f. polite request 10. He must be on time to make a good impression. ➔ a. obligation Activity 3.9: Sentence Paraphrase Matching 1. Tinsae must write a report tomorrow. ➔ c. Tinsae will have to write a report tomorrow. 2. Tinsae couldn't write it yesterday. ➔ e. Tinsae wasn't able to write it yesterday. 3. Rahel says she can help him tomorrow. ➔ d. Rahel says she will be able to help him tomorrow. 4. She has to help him, or the report will not be finished on time. ➔ a. She needs to help him, or the report will not be finished on time. 5. Rahel's boss says she may help Jack. ➔ b. Rahel's boss says she is allowed to help Jack. Activity 3.10: Easter Island Text Completion Scientists believe that the original inhabitants may have landed by accident. Around 100 people may have discovered the island on the western coast... Scientists agree that the inhabitants must have used up all the food on the island and finally all died. The statues are famous, but nobody knows why... The statues might have been gods or Easter Island could have been part of a much bigger island. The statues are very large and heavy, so they can't have been easy to move. Scientists still do not know how the inhabitants might have done this. Activity 3.11: Flooding Gap-Fill Solutions 1. might be (or may get) 2. can't have 3. could take 4. must be 5. can't be 6. must be 7. may get 8. may not have Activity 3.14: Environmental Vocabulary - Ozone Depletion: Thinning of Earth's ozone layer due to pollutants (የኦዞን ንጣፍ መሸርሸር) - Deforestation: Large-scale clearing of trees without replanting (የደን ጭፍጨፋ) - Desertification: Degradation of fertile land into desert (በረሃማነት) - Urban Sprawl: Uncontrolled expansion of cities into rural land (የከተሞች ያልተመጠነ መስፋፋት) - Acid Rain: Rainfall made acidic by atmospheric pollution (አሲዳማ ዝናብ) - Loss of Biodiversity: Reduction in biological diversity of species (የብዝሃ-ሕይወት መጥፋት) - Solutions: Recycling (ቆሻሻን መልሶ መጠቀም), Alternative energy (ታዳሽ ኃይል), Hybrid cars ========================================= 4. ADVANCED GRAMMAR RULES, EXAM PITFALLS & SPECIAL CASES ========================================= Rule 1: Distinguishing 'Must have + V3' vs 'Should have + V3' - Must have + V3 (Logical Conclusion): Indicates a logical conclusion based on available evidence. It means "it is almost certain that this happened." - Should have + V3 (Regret / Unfulfilled Action): Indicates a criticism, regret, or a recommended past action that was NOT performed. ❌ Incorrect: He scored 100% on his difficult exam. He should have studied hard. ✅ Correct: He scored 100% on his difficult exam. He must have studied hard. (ከፍተኛ ውጤት ስለአመጣ በጥሩ ሁኔታ አጠናቆ መሆን አለበት) Rule 2: Negative Past Logical Certainty ('Can't have + V3') Academic English exams strictly forbid using must not have + V3 to express past impossibility. You must use can't have + V3 or couldn't have + V3. ❌ Incorrect: They lacked modern cranes, so they must not have moved those massive stones easily. ✅ Correct: They lacked modern cranes, so moving those massive stones can't have been easy. Rule 3: Past General Ability ('Could') vs Past Specific Success ('Was/Were able to') - Use could for general skills possessed over time in the past (e.g., I could swim when I was ten). - Use was/were able to or managed to for a specific, difficult accomplishment on a particular past instance. ❌ Incorrect: The fire spread fast, but everyone could escape safely. ✅ Correct: The fire spread fast, but everyone was able to escape safely. Rule 4: Difference Between 'Mustn't' and 'Don't have to' - Mustn't (Prohibition): Means it is forbidden, illegal, or harmful to do something. - Don't have to (Lack of Necessity): Means doing something is unnecessary, but optional if desired. - Example 1: You mustn't smoke near fuel tanks. (Strictly forbidden) - Example 2: You don't have to bring a camera; we will take photos for you. (Optional) Rule 5: No Double Modals or Infinitives after Modals Never chain pure modal verbs together (will can, must should) or follow them with infinitive 'to'. ❌ Incorrect: Governments must to enforce strict laws. ✅ Correct: Governments must enforce strict laws. ❌ Incorrect: He will can finish the project tomorrow. ✅ Correct: He will be able to finish the project tomorrow. ========================================= 5. PRACTICE EXAM QUESTIONS WITH DETAILED EXPLANATIONS ========================================= Question 1: The water level in the reservoir ________ rapidly during last year's severe drought, dropping by over 50%. A. refuted B. plummeted C. transformed D. sprawled Correct Answer: B. plummeted Explanation: 'Plummeted' means to decrease or fall sharply and rapidly, which accurately fits the context of a 50% loss in water levels. Question 2: Look at those massive stone monuments on Easter Island! The ancient islanders ________ exceptional engineering knowledge to build them. A. should have possessed B. must have possessed C. can't have possessed D. ought to possess Correct Answer: B. must have possessed Explanation: The physical existence of massive monuments provides clear proof for a strong positive logical deduction in the past (`must have + V3`). Question 3: The ground in the valley is completely parched and dry. It ________ rained here for several months. A. must have B. should have C. can't have D. might have Correct Answer: C. can't have Explanation: The dry, parched ground serves as strong evidence that rainfall was logically impossible in the recent past (`can't have + V3`). Question 4: Many farmers strongly ________ the argument that current drought conditions are purely caused by global climate change. A. acute B. eerily C. refute D. sprawl Correct Answer: C. refute Explanation: 'Refute' is a transitive verb meaning to disprove or reject a claim with counter-arguments. Question 5: We failed to prepare adequate emergency supplies before the flood hit. We ________ more drinking water in advance. A. must have stored B. can't have stored C. should have stored D. may have stored Correct Answer: C. should have stored Explanation: 'Should have + V3' expresses regret or criticism about a sensible past action that was unfortunately omitted. Question 6: You ________ wear a seatbelt while driving on high-speed highways; it is a strict legal requirement. A. should B. may C. have to D. could Correct Answer: C. have to Explanation: 'Have to' is used to express external obligations created by laws, regulations, or statutory mandates.
